terms: Aims
Long-term general goals giving direction; e.g. 'be the leading UK organic food retailer'.
Objectives
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound (SMART) targets that operationalise aims.
Profit maximisation
Aim to make as much profit as possible; classical assumption but rarely sole goal in modern firms.
Social objectives
Goals beyond profit: ethical sourcing, environmental sustainability; e.g. Patagonia's '1% for the Planet'.
Stakeholder vs shareholder
Shareholder model (Friedman 1970) prioritises owners; stakeholder model considers customers, staff, suppliers, community.
Survival
Common short-term aim for start-ups and during economic downturns; focuses on cash flow over profit.

Business cycle
The repeating pattern of growth, boom, recession and recovery in an economy, which changes the level of demand for most products.
Environmental and ethical influences
Pressure from laws, consumers and pressure groups pushes businesses to cut pollution and behave ethically, sometimes raising their costs.
Exchange rate
The price of one currency in terms of another; a stronger currency makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home.
Fiscal policy
Government decisions on taxation and public spending; higher taxes reduce consumers' disposable income and can lower demand for businesses.
Government economic objectives
Governments aim for low inflation, low unemployment, economic growth and a healthy balance of payments, using policy to pursue them.
Interest rates
The cost of borrowing money; higher rates increase loan repayments, discourage business investment and reduce consumer spending on credit.
Business plan
Document setting out objectives, market research, finances and operations; used to attract investment and guide management.
Enterprise
Process of identifying an opportunity, organising resources and taking the risk of starting a business.
Entrepreneur
Person who takes financial risk to start and run a business in pursuit of profit; Schumpeter (1934) called them 'creative destroyers'.
Innovation vs invention
Invention is creating something new; innovation is bringing it successfully to market and gaining adoption.
Risk vs reward
Entrepreneurs invest time and money expecting profit, market share and personal satisfaction; failure rate around 60% within 3 years (ONS).
Spotting opportunity
Identifying unmet customer needs or new market gaps; James Dyson identified bag-clogging issue, launching 1993 cyclone vacuum.
Capacity utilisation
Actual output / maximum output x 100; high utilisation lowers unit fixed costs but risks bottlenecks.
Just-in-time
Inventory arrives only as needed; reduces holding costs but requires reliable suppliers; vulnerable to disruption (COVID, Suez 2021).
Kaizen
Japanese for continuous improvement; small ongoing changes from all employees, central to lean philosophy.
Lean production
Toyota (1948 onwards): minimise waste in time, materials, defects; just-in-time stock and kaizen improvement.
Operations
Activities transforming inputs into outputs of goods or services; aim to maximise efficiency and quality.
Productivity
Output per worker or per hour; UK output per hour was 16% below the G7 average in 2023 (ONS).

operations-finance-and-influences-on-bus.d: Operations, Finance and Influences on Business
terms: Break-even
The level of output where total revenue equals total costs, calculated as fixed costs divided by contribution per unit.
Cash flow
The money moving into and out of a business over time; even profitable firms fail if they cannot pay their bills when due.
Ethical and environmental influences
Acting ethically and reducing environmental damage can raise costs but also attract customers and protect a business's reputation.
Production methods
Job production makes one-off items, batch production makes groups of similar products, and flow production makes identical items continuously on a line.
Quality control vs assurance
Quality control checks finished goods for faults, while quality assurance prevents faults by building checks into every production stage.
Sources of finance
Businesses raise money from retained profit, loans, overdrafts, share capital, trade credit and crowdfunding, each with different costs and risks.
